notes:
Here are verse-by-verse notes on Psalm 126, based only on the pages I could read. Some areas had little or nothing, and I say so at the end.

---

## Background (whole psalm)

- **Setting:** Guzik says most readers link the psalm to the return from exile under Ezra and Nehemiah. He adds that it could also describe David coming back to Jerusalem after Absalom's revolt. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-126/
- **Date:** Ellicott says the psalm gives no exact date. All that is certain is that it was written after the exile. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/psalms/126.htm
- **Two halves:** Maclaren (Expositor's Bible) says verses 1–3 rejoice that the restoration has begun, and verses 4–6 pray for it to be finished and expect that it will be. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/expositors/psalms/126.htm
- **A reading about Christ:** An older writer quoted in Spurgeon's *Treasury of David* reads the whole psalm as being about humanity's captivity to sin, death and the devil, and about the redemption Christ bought. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/spurgeon_charles/tod/ps126.cfm

---

**v. 1 – "When the LORD restored the captives of Zion, we were like dreamers"**

*Traditional reading*
- Guzik: the people were happily amazed at God's goodness. It seemed too good to be true, but it was true. He cites Poole, who links this to other moments when people could not believe good news, such as Luke 24:11 and Acts 12:9. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-126/
- Matthew Henry: Cyrus freed the captives for political reasons, yet it was still the Lord's doing, as He had promised long before. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Psa/Psa_126.cfm
- A writer in Spurgeon's *Treasury* explains the surprise: the great Eastern empires never let deported peoples go home, and he says no other nation in history except the Jews returned to rebuild its cities. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/spurgeon_charles/tod/ps126.cfm

*Where interpreters differ*
- **Gill (labelled Baptist and Calvinist on StudyLight):** the past tense may stand for the future, making the verse a prophecy. It may point both to the return from Babylon and to a future conversion of the Jewish people. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/psalms-126.html
- Another writer in Spurgeon's *Treasury* expects the psalm to be sung again when Israel is restored in the future. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/spurgeon_charles/tod/ps126.cfm

*Translation questions*
- Ellicott: the Hebrew wording here differs from verse 4 and can mean "brought back the returned of Zion." The Greek (LXX) and Latin (Vulgate) translations read "as if consoled" instead of "like dreamers." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/psalms/126.htm
- Utley (bible.org): some scholars suggest a small change to the Hebrew text, giving "restores the fortunes of Zion." On that reading, "fortunes" would mean renewed prosperity, a visible sign that God's covenant was restored. https://bible.org/seriespage/psalm-126
- The BSB footnotes give the alternatives "restored the fortunes of Zion" and "like those restored to health." https://biblehub.com/bsb/psalms/126.htm

*Catholic / early church*
- **Augustine:** we became captives by being "sold under sin," and Christ's innocent blood redeemed us. The exile in Babylon is a picture ("shadow") of this, and Babylon stands for this confused world. Following the Latin "as those that are comforted," he says we are comforted in hope while we still mourn. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/1801126.htm

---

**v. 2 – Laughter, shouts of joy, and the nations' testimony**

*Traditional reading*
- Spurgeon (cited by Guzik): the mercy was so unexpected that they could only laugh, and their mouths were full because their hearts were full. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-126/
- Matthew Henry: the return gave honour to people who had been despised. It also forced those who worshipped other gods to admit God's power. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Psa/Psa_126.cfm
- Ellicott: "singing" about the restoration is a frequent theme in Isaiah. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/psalms/126.htm
- R. Tuck (Pulpit Commentary): seeing the exiles' joy, the nations could no longer think Israel's God never forgives. It showed that God pities even while He punishes. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/psalms-126.html

*Lutheran*
- **Luther (quoted by Spurgeon and Guzik):** the gospel is "nothing else but laughter and joy." This joy belongs to those who feel their captivity to sin and death. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/spurgeon_charles/tod/ps126.cfm, https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-126/

*Catholic / early church*
- **Augustine:** the "mouth" filled with joy is the inner mouth of the heart, which he links to Jesus' teaching in Matthew 15. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/1801126.htm

---

**v. 3 – "The LORD has done great things for us"**

*Traditional reading*
- Maclaren: the singer picks up the nations' grudging admission and in a way thanks them for teaching him the words. Their "for them" becomes his "for us." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/expositors/psalms/126.htm, https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-126/
- Guzik: "we are glad" is a calm, confident joy, not worked-up excitement. He lists Boice's four occasions of such joy: salvation, spiritual victory, fellowship, and a new work for God. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-126/
- Spurgeon (Verse Expositions): he likens joys like this to a deposit (the "earnest") of the inheritance to come. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/spe/psalms-126.html

*Catholic / early church*
- **Augustine:** the restored people did nothing for themselves except sell themselves into sin. The Redeemer did the great things. He sees the verse fulfilled as people around the world come into the Church. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/1801126.htm

---

**v. 4 – "Restore our captives, O LORD, like streams in the Negev"**

*Why pray this if the captives are already back?*
- Pulpit Commentary: the work was not half done, since not half the nation had returned. Those in the land were only "a remnant." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/126-4.htm
- Barnes: the exiles came back in waves over many years, under Cyrus, Darius and Xerxes, so the prayer asks God to finish the work. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/126-4.htm
- Utley calls the verse hard to explain. This is one reason the Jewish Publication Society translation reads it as a prayer for renewed prosperity. https://bible.org/seriespage/psalm-126
- Guzik: the second half does not deny the joy of the first. It sees that much work remains. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-126/

*The image of the Negev streams*
- Ellicott: the picture is of dry gullies in the south suddenly filling in the rainy season. The poet prays for streams of returning exiles to pour into the empty land. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/psalms/126.htm
- Guzik: these sudden flash floods picture a mighty, sudden work of God. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-126/
- Other views of the image:
  - A writer in Spurgeon's *Treasury* pictures small irrigation channels instead. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/spurgeon_charles/tod/ps126.cfm
  - Adam Clarke thinks the Nile is probably meant. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/126-4.html

*Reformed and Baptist*
- **Calvin:** many take the sense to be that the return would be as welcome as water flowing through a desert. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/126-4.html
- **Geneva Study Bible:** it is no harder for God to rescue His people than to make rivers run in the wilderness. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/126-4.htm
- **Gill:** the verse can be read as a prayer for the Redeemer to free people from sin, Satan and the law, or for the conversion of the Jews in the last days. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/psalms-126.html

*A "second blessing" application (Pulpit Commentary homilies)*
- S. Conway calls this verse "the prayer for a second blessing" and says the soul longs for a fuller salvation. He uses the phrase as a sermon application; he does not develop it as a doctrine. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/psalms-126.html

*Catholic / early church*
- **Augustine:** he follows the Latin, which links the streams to the south wind. Our sins froze us like ice. The warm south wind is the Holy Spirit, who melts the ice when sins are forgiven, so that we run home like torrents. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/1801126.htm
- Ellicott notes that this "south wind" reading comes from the ancient translations, which pictured a frozen stream melting rather than a dry riverbed filling. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/psalms/126.htm
- Keil and Delitzsch: if you translate the verse as Jerome does, following the Greek, the picture no longer fits. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/126-4.htm

---

**v. 5 – "Those who sow in tears will reap with shouts of joy"**

*Traditional reading*
- Boice and Kidner (cited by Guzik): the two pictures go together. The streams in verse 4 are sudden and unearned. The harvest in verses 5–6 comes slowly, after hard work, and people have a real part to play. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-126/
- Pulpit Commentary: "sowing in tears" is the hard work of rebuilding Israel (Ezra 3:12–13), and the joy is seeing that work bear fruit. https://studylight.org/commentaries/tpc/psalms-126.html
- Keil and Delitzsch: the tearful sowing stands for laying the foundations again amid sorrow. In general terms it matches "Blessed are those who mourn" (Matthew 5:4). https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/126-4.htm
- Matthew Henry: weeping must not stop us sowing. Some tears are themselves the seed: sorrow for sin, sympathy for the suffering church, and tenderness in prayer. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Psa/Psa_126.cfm
- Spurgeon: the verse is "an inspired proverb." The promise belongs specially to sowing *in tears*, and "winners of souls are first weepers for souls." https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/spurgeon_charles/tod/ps126.cfm
- John Piper (Desiring God): sowing seed is not sad in itself. The tears come from other troubles in life, and the work must be done anyway. https://www.desiringgod.org/solid-joys/talk-to-your-tears
- TGC podcast: the farmers may be weeping over the national crisis behind verse 4, or the verse may be a proverb that is always true. Either way, God's people serve faithfully while they wait for Him to act. https://www.thegospelcoalition.org/podcasts/word-of-the-week/when-dry-riverbeds-flow-again-psalm-126/

*Catholic / early church*
- **Augustine:** the seed is good works, especially works of mercy and giving to the poor. He links this to Galatians 6:9 and 2 Corinthians 9:6. Even a person with nothing can sow good will. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/1801126.htm
- **Thomas Aquinas:** in discussing the sacrament of Penance, he quotes a gloss (a standard medieval note) on this verse about good will being rewarded with peace. https://www.newadvent.org/summa/4084.htm
- **Tertullian:** he uses the verse to argue that the Creator God of the Old Testament first promised that mourners would laugh, a promise Christ repeats in the Beatitudes. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/03124.htm

---

**v. 6 – Going out weeping, returning with sheaves**

*Traditional reading*
- Pulpit Commentary: the Hebrew is literally "going he goes and weeping… coming he comes with a cry of joy." He weeps every step, scattering seed from his bag. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/psalms/126.htm
- Kidner (cited by Guzik): the doubled verbs stress certainty, "will surely come home." https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-126/
- Ellicott: this extends the picture of verse 5 rather than repeating it. It shows patient labour and a harvest in proportion to it, and should be compared with Haggai. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/psalms/126.htm
- VanGemeren (cited by Guzik): the people could not sit and wait. They had to sow, as Haggai urged them to. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-126/
- A writer in Spurgeon's *Treasury* stresses that the harvest is certain because the verbs are flat promises, not possibilities. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/spurgeon_charles/tod/ps126.cfm
- Two applications quoted in Spurgeon's *Treasury*:
  - Christ is the sower in tears, "the Man of sorrows."
  - The verse pictures a minister who waters the gospel with tears and prayers and returns with his sheaves at the last day.
  https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/spurgeon_charles/tod/ps126.cfm

*Catholic / early church*
- **Augustine:** a farmer goes out to sow even in bitter weather. In the same way, do not put off good works; sow while you weep. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/1801126.htm

---

## What I couldn't find

- **Differences between Protestant traditions:** The sources show differences of emphasis, not clear denominational splits. Some read the psalm historically (Barnes, Pulpit), some about Christ and redemption (Gill, the *Treasury* writers), and some about a future restoration of Israel (Gill). I found no Methodist or Wesleyan source (wesley.nnu.edu, seedbed.com) and no Pentecostal one. The Lutheran material is only Luther as quoted by Spurgeon. Anglican material is only George Horne, quoted in Spurgeon's *Treasury* (he is not labelled Anglican there).
- **Modern scholarship:** I could not reach netbible.org or bibleodyssey.org. The textual points above come from Ellicott, Expositor's, Keil and Delitzsch, and bible.org.
- **Orthodox (oca.org) and catholic.com:** nothing found.
- **Prosperity or "seed-faith" teaching on verses 5–6:** I found no page that discusses it, so I have left it out.
